result: The study used volume electron microscopy (FIB/SEM) to analyze human MEC tissue from three individuals (ages 40-66, postmortem delays <4 hr), obtaining 63 stacks of images and fully reconstructing 12,974 synapses in 3D across all MEC layers (I, II-is, II-ni, III, Va/b, Vc, VI), with 8,605 synapses ultimately analyzed after exclusion criteria.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C48-C49, C62-C66, and C255-C257 collectively describe the methodology, sample characteristics, and data collection scope. The tissue source is well-documented with appropriate ethical approval, the technical approach (FIB/SEM) is clearly stated, and quantitative metrics (number of stacks, synapses reconstructed, volumes analyzed) are provided with supporting supplementary data. The methodology is rigorous and transparent.

result: Neuropil constituted 86-96% of grey matter volume across all MEC layers, with cell bodies occupying 1-9% and blood vessels 3-6%, consistent with values from other human cortical regions.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 provide quantitative volume fraction data supported by Figure 1 and supplementary files. Claims C151-C152 contextualize these findings by comparing them to prior studies in human neocortex and hippocampus. The measurements are based on established stereological methods (Cavalieri principle) and show consistency with previous literature.

result: Mean synaptic density across all MEC layers was 0.41 synapses/μm³, with no statistically significant differences between layers (p>0.05), though deep layers (Va/b: 0.35, VI: 0.36) showed slightly lower densities than superficial layers (I: 0.47, II-III: 0.40-0.44), and MEC densities were lower than other human cortical regions studied with identical methods.
evaluation: Claims C74-C79 and C144-C148 present synaptic density measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis). The lack of significant differences between layers is properly reported, and comparisons with other cortical regions (C146) are supported by citations to studies using identical methods. The conclusion about layer-specific analysis importance (C148) is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: The AS:SS ratio averaged 94:6 across all MEC layers (range 93:7 to 96:4), with no significant differences between layers, consistent with established knowledge that cortical neuropil has predominantly asymmetric (excitatory) over symmetric (inhibitory) synapses, though this study focused exclusively on neuropil synapses and did not analyze perisomatic innervation.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 provide the AS:SS ratio data supported by Figure 1D and Table 1. Claims C153-C154 confirm consistency with prior literature. Claims C155-C158 appropriately acknowledge limitations in functional interpretation and scope (neuropil only, not perisomatic). The findings are well-supported but the authors correctly note interpretive challenges.

result: Synaptic spatial distribution in the MEC neuropil was indistinguishable from random in most samples (51/63 stacks), with mean intersynaptic distance of 867 nm and no significant differences between layers, consistent with findings in other human cortical areas and suggesting that while axons achieve layer-specific targeting, synapse placement within layers may be spatially random.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 and C159-C167 describe spatial distribution analysis using F, G, and K functions compared to complete spatial randomness (CSR) models. The methodology is appropriate, results are quantified (51/63 stacks random), and comparisons with other human cortical regions (C163) support generalizability. The interpretation (C165) about layer-specific but not synapse-specific targeting is speculative but reasonable. Claims C166-C167 appropriately acknowledge exceptions and potential technical explanations.

result: Asymmetric synapses (AS) were significantly larger than symmetric synapses (SS) across all layers (mean AS: 119,242 nm², SS: 71,384 nm², p<0.0001-0.05 depending on layer), with layer-specific differences in AS size (smallest in layer VI: 99,489 nm², largest in layers III and Va/b: 130,268-136,111 nm²), supporting the idea that this characteristic is highly conserved in human cerebral cortex.
evaluation: Claims C87-C93 and C170-C172 present synaptic size measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's test) and are supported by Figure 3, Table 1, and supplementary data. The finding that AS are larger than SS is consistent across all layers and with prior literature. Layer-specific differences are statistically significant and properly reported. The conclusion about conservation across human cortex (C172) is supported by comparisons with prior studies.

result: The size distribution of both AS and SS fit a log-normal probability distribution in all MEC layers and when pooled together, consistent with previous human brain studies and suggesting this is a general characteristic of mammalian cortical synapses.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 and C173-C175 describe goodness-of-fit analyses showing log-normal distributions for synaptic size data, supported by supplementary file 1e. The finding is consistent with prior human brain studies (C174) and the conclusion about this being a general mammalian characteristic (C175) is a reasonable inference. The acknowledgment that the fit was better for AS due to larger sample size (C96) shows appropriate caution.

result: The majority of synapses in the MEC exhibited macular shape (84% overall), with complex-shaped synapses being consistently larger than macular synapses for both AS and SS (p<0.0001 for AS in all layers), and layer VI showing the lowest proportion of macular synapses (78% for AS, 59% for SS) while layer II-is showed the highest (88%).
evaluation: Claims C98-C106 and C184-C187 describe synaptic shape analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney, chi-square) supported by Figure 4 and supplementary data. The predominance of macular synapses and their smaller size compared to complex synapses is well-documented. Layer-specific differences are statistically significant. The findings are consistent with prior research in other brain regions (C185).

result: Considering all MEC layers, 59.3% of synapses were AS on dendritic spine heads, 34.3% were AS on dendritic shafts, 5.1% were SS on shafts, with smaller percentages on spine necks, and layer VI showed the highest proportion of AS on spine heads (76.2%) while layer Va/b had the lowest (52.9%, p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C107-C115 and C193 provide detailed quantitative data on postsynaptic targets supported by Figure 6 and supplementary files. The measurements are comprehensive, covering all major postsynaptic target types. Statistical comparisons between layers are appropriate (chi-square test) and significant differences are properly reported. The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: The majority of SS were found on dendritic shafts (85.7%), while AS showed a strong preference for dendritic spine heads, with the AS:SS ratio being 99:1 on spines versus 87:13 on shafts (p<0.0001), consistent with findings across all human cortical regions analyzed to date using the same methods.
evaluation: Claims C116-C121 and C201-C203 describe the differential targeting of AS and SS to postsynaptic structures with appropriate statistical testing (chi-square, p<0.0001). The finding of preferential AS targeting to spines and SS to shafts is well-established in the literature (C201) and the consistency across human cortical regions (C203) strengthens the conclusion. The data are supported by Figure 6 and supplementary files.

result: The vast majority of dendritic spines (96%) contained only one AS, with no significant differences between layers (p>0.0001), and interestingly, spines with one AS and one SS (0.73%) were more common than spines with a single SS (0.50%), with AS on AS:SS multisynaptic spines being 30% larger than single AS (p<0.01).
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 and C208-C214 describe multisynaptic spine analysis with appropriate statistics. The finding that 96% of spines contain single AS is consistent with prior studies in other cortical areas (C209-C210). The observation about AS:SS spines being more common than single SS spines (C124) is interesting and well-documented. The size difference for AS on multisynaptic spines (C214, C129) is statistically significant and relates to established knowledge about synaptic stability (C211-C213).

result: For AS, synapses on dendritic spine heads and shafts had similar mean areas (127,956 nm² vs 120,978 nm²), while AS on spine necks were significantly smaller (66,435 nm², p<0.001), with layer-specific differences showing Va/b had the largest AS on both heads (148,730 nm²) and shafts (143,122 nm²) while layer VI had the smallest on heads (105,948 nm²) and layer I the smallest on shafts (99,960 nm²).
evaluation: Claims C125-C128 and C206-C207 present synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target with appropriate statistical testing (Dunn's test) supported by Figure 6-supplement 3 and supplementary data. The finding that AS on spine heads and shafts are similar in size (C125, C206) differs from some other cortical regions (C204-C205), which the authors appropriately note as a potential specialization (C207). Layer-specific differences are statistically significant and well-documented.

result: The distribution of macular AS on spine heads versus shafts was 61:39, similar to the overall AS distribution (63:37), but complex-shaped AS showed a significantly higher proportion on spine heads (75:25, p<0.0001), with layer VI exhibiting the highest proportions of both macular (78%) and complex-shaped (85%) synapses on spines.
evaluation: Claims C131-C135 and C215-C218 describe the relationship between synaptic shape and postsynaptic target with appropriate statistical testing (chi-square). The finding that complex synapses preferentially target spine heads (C134, C217) is statistically significant and biologically meaningful. The calculation that complex synapses on spine heads are ~15% higher than expected (C218) is a reasonable inference from the data. Layer VI's distinctiveness (C135) is well-documented.

result: Smaller macular synapses were more frequent on spine heads than shafts (p<0.0001), while smaller complex-shaped synapses were more frequent on shafts than spine heads (p<0.0001), with complex AS on spine heads being larger than those on shafts, and macular AS on shafts being larger than those on spine heads.
evaluation: Claims C136-C137 and C219 describe frequency distribution analyses of synaptic size by shape and postsynaptic target using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (p<0.0001), supported by Figure 7. The statistical testing is appropriate and the findings are clearly presented. The differential size distributions by shape and target location represent a detailed characterization of synaptic organization.

result: Little interindividual variability was observed for synaptic characteristics, with the SAS area of AS showing the highest coefficient of variation (3.3-19.6% across layers), and only two statistically significant differences found between individuals (SAS area of AS in layer II-is and complex AS in layer VI, both between cases AB2 and AB7), with SS characteristics being particularly uniform across individuals, layers, and image stacks.
evaluation: Claims C138-C140 and C248-C252 describe interindividual variability analysis using coefficient of variation and statistical comparisons (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's test) supported by Table 2, supplementary files, and figure supplements. The finding of low variability is well-documented and the specific exceptions (C140) are properly identified. The consistency of SS characteristics (C251-C252) is noted and compared to prior literature. The analysis is thorough and appropriately cautious.

result: The MEC exhibits a distinct set of synaptic features differentiating it from other human cortical areas, while also revealing common patterns across mammalian brains (such as proportion of synaptic types and shapes), with ultrastructural characteristics being predominantly similar within the MEC though layers I and VI show several distinct characteristics.
evaluation: Claims C6, C141-C143, and C253 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are supported by the comprehensive dataset showing: (1) distinct features like lower synaptic density than other cortical regions (C146-C147), (2) conserved features like AS:SS ratios and log-normal size distributions consistent with other regions (C142, C153-C154, C173-C175), and (3) layer-specific differences particularly in layers I and VI (C8, C143, C234-C236). The conclusions are well-supported by the data presented.

result: Synaptic size correlates with release probability, synaptic strength, efficacy, and plasticity, and with the number of receptors in the PSD, with the MEC showing layer-specific components in synaptic size (smallest in layers I and VI, largest in layers III and Va/b), though caution is needed when correlating receptor densities with synaptic size due to extrasynaptic receptors.
evaluation: Claims C168-C169 and C178-C180 establish the functional significance of synaptic size based on well-cited prior literature. Claims C176-C177 present the layer-specific findings from this study. Claim C181 attempts to correlate findings with prior receptor density studies, but claims C182-C183 appropriately urge caution due to extrasynaptic receptors. The functional interpretation is reasonable but appropriately cautious about limitations.

result: Complex-shaped synapses have larger AMPA and NMDA receptor populations than macular synapses, making them more powerful and stable and contributing to long-lasting memory-related functionality, while macular synapses may play a crucial role in synaptic plasticity, suggesting that the higher proportion of complex-shaped synapses in layer VI may indicate higher synaptic strengths while the prevalence of macular synapses in layer II may suggest lower release probability and synaptic strength.
evaluation: Claims C188-C190 and C220-C222 are supported by citations to prior literature establishing the functional properties of different synapse shapes. However, claims C191-C192 and C221 are speculative interpretations of the functional implications of the shape distributions observed in this study. While the speculation is reasonable and based on established principles, the study did not directly measure receptor populations, synaptic strength, or plasticity in the MEC. The functional interpretations go beyond what the morphological data alone can support.

result: The membrane potential of postsynaptic neurons is modulated differently depending on whether synapses are on spines or shafts, making variations in these proportions functionally significant, with the MEC showing 60% AS on spines and 34% on shafts, which differs from some other cortical regions (e.g., 67-74% on spines in Brodmann areas 17, 21, 24, 38, 3b), suggesting microanatomical specialization of synaptic structure in the neuropil.
evaluation: Claim C194 establishes the functional significance of postsynaptic target location based on cited literature. Claim C195 is a reasonable inference. Claims C196-C199 provide comparative data from prior studies using the same methods, and claim C200 draws the conclusion about microanatomical specialization. The comparison is valid because the same methods were used, and the differences in proportions are substantial enough to suggest regional specialization. The conclusion is well-supported.

result: Previous studies using transmission electron microscopy reported synaptic densities in human EC layers III and V that were ~30% lower (0.32 and 0.27 synapses/μm³) than the present study's findings, with differences potentially stemming from methodological variations including layer subdivision, subject age, postmortem delay, and density estimation methods (2D size-frequency method vs. 3D FIB/SEM).
evaluation: Claims C149-C150 compare the current findings with prior work by Scheff et al. (1993) and discuss potential methodological reasons for the differences. The comparison is appropriate and the discussion of methodological differences (layer subdivision, subject characteristics, 2D vs 3D methods) is reasonable. The authors correctly note that FIB/SEM provides actual 3D counts while the size-frequency method estimates from 2D sections, which could account for the discrepancy.

result: Despite the MEC's complexity in cytoarchitecture, connectivity, and function (with heterogeneous neuronal populations and diverse local and intercortical connections), the similarity of ultrastructural synaptic characteristics across layers is surprising and may indicate that parameters like synaptic density and AS:SS ratio do not depend on cytoarchitecture or connectivity, though studies in other regions (hippocampus, BA38) suggest synaptic characteristics can be influenced by layer-specific innervation patterns.
evaluation: Claims C223-C229 establish the complexity of the MEC based on prior literature (C224-C229 supported by citations and Figure 8). Claims C240-C241 present the interpretation that synaptic parameters may be independent of cytoarchitecture/connectivity. Claims C242-C245 appropriately note that few studies have examined this question and cite counterexamples where layer-specific innervation does influence synaptic characteristics. The discussion is balanced and acknowledges both the surprising uniformity and the exceptions found in other regions.

result: Analysis of MEC layer II showed no differences in any synaptic parameter between the neuropil of cell islands and non-island (transition) areas, with results very similar to a previous study that analyzed layer II without distinguishing these zones (synaptic density 0.40 vs. 0.42-0.44 synapses/μm³).
evaluation: Claims C230-C233 describe the layer II analysis comparing cell islands and transition zones. The finding of no differences is clearly stated (C231) and compared to prior work by the same group (C232-C233). The consistency between studies strengthens the conclusion. This addresses an important question about the functional significance of the distinctive cytoarchitecture of layer II.

result: Layer VI stood out in many synaptic parameters, having comparable synaptic density to other layers but the smallest synapses overall, the smallest macular and complex-shaped AS, the lowest proportion of macular synapses (78%), and the highest proportion of synapses on dendritic spine heads (76%), with this layer containing diverse cell types and receiving projections from multiple regions including hippocampus, medial frontal and orbitofrontal cortex, thalamus, and claustrum, suggesting these synaptic peculiarities may critically impact information processing.
evaluation: Claims C234-C236 summarize the distinctive synaptic characteristics of layer VI documented throughout the results. Claims C237-C238 provide context about the cellular composition and connectivity of layer VI based on prior literature. Claim C239 is a speculative but reasonable inference about functional implications. The characterization of layer VI as distinctive is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence from the study.

result: Interindividual variability is a crucial aspect of human brain studies, with numerous studies documenting structural and functional variability in human cerebral cortex, and future studies on synaptic nanoconnectivity of different layers in additional brain regions could confirm whether there is a commonly shared trend across the human cortex.
evaluation: Claim C246 states the importance of considering interindividual variability. Claim C247 is supported by a citation to prior literature. Claim C254 is a reasonable suggestion for future research. These claims provide appropriate context for interpreting the study's findings of relatively low variability and suggest productive directions for future work.
